identity.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free

problem.claim: The work investigates how gating affects softmax attention in large language models.

gap.claim: Existing literature rarely examines the specific effects of gating.

contributions.claim: A systematic comparison of 30 gating variants across 15B Mixture-of-Experts and 1.7B dense models trained on 3.5 trillion tokens.
A head-specific sigmoid gate applied after Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA).
The reported effectiveness is attributed to non-linearity over softmax attention’s low-rank mapping and query-dependent sparse gating of SDPA outputs.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a systematic investigation of gating-augmented softmax attention and identify a simple post-SDPA gating modification as consistently beneficial in their comparisons.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that head-specific post-SDPA sigmoid gating consistently improves performance.
The authors report improved training stability, tolerance of larger learning rates, and improved scaling properties.
The authors report that sparse gating mitigates massive activation and attention sink, while improving long-context extrapolation performance.

narrative_sequence.summary: Gating is widespread, but its specific effects are rarely examined.
The authors systematically compare 30 variants across large MoE and dense language models trained on a 3.5-trillion-token dataset.
A head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA is reported to improve performance, stability, learning-rate tolerance, and scaling.
The authors link the result to non-linearity and query-dependent sparse modulation, reporting mitigation of activation and attention-sink issues plus better long-context extrapolation.
Codes and models are released, and the most effective SDPA output gate is used in Qwen3-Next models.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a broad variant comparison with a proposed mechanistic attribution based on gating position and computational variants.

lessons.interpretation: Comparing controlled design variants can support a more explanatory account than reporting aggregate performance alone.
lessons.application: When introducing an architectural modification, compare placement and computational alternatives, then state which observed differences motivate the mechanism claimed.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the study cannot isolate variants or lacks evidence connecting the comparisons to the proposed mechanism.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects the method’s reported benefits to concrete training and inference-related phenomena, including stability, learning-rate tolerance, massive activation, attention sink, and long-context extrapolation.

lessons.interpretation: Linking headline gains to operational behaviors makes an architectural claim more diagnostically useful.
lessons.application: Report whether a proposed change affects specific failure modes or scaling behaviors, alongside general performance.
lessons.exception: Do not generalize this practice when those behaviors are not measured or are outside the method’s intended scope.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide numerical effect sizes, baselines, statistical treatment, or detailed experimental conditions.
The abstract does not specify which model scales or tasks yield each reported benefit.
The abstract reports mechanistic attribution but does not provide the underlying analyses needed to assess it here.
